questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If the police had investigated sooner, the suspect wouldn't be free now.
If the police investigated sooner, the suspect wouldn't be free now.
If the police had investigated sooner, the suspect wouldn't have been free now.
If the police had investigated sooner, the suspect won't be free now.
questions.explanation: Mixed conditional: If + past perfect (past condition), would + base verb (present result): 'If the police had investigated..., the suspect wouldn't be free now.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Crime rates will keep rising unless the city won't hire more officers.
Crime rates will keep rising unless the city hires more officers.
Crime rates will keep rising unless that the city hires more officers.
Crime rates will keep rising without the city hires more officers.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if...not' and is followed by an affirmative clause: 'unless the city hires more officers.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Several new laws has been passed this year.
Several new laws have passed this year.
Several new laws have been passed this year.
Several new laws have being passed this year.
questions.explanation: Present perfect passive: have/has been + past participle: 'have been passed this year.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This legal loophole should closed immediately.
This legal loophole should being closed immediately.
This legal loophole should be close immediately.
This legal loophole should be closed immediately.
questions.explanation: Modal passive: modal + be + past participle: 'should be closed immediately.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "Please remain silent during the trial.")
options: The judge told us to remain silent during the trial.
The judge told us remain silent during the trial.
The judge said us to remain silent during the trial.
The judge told us that remain silent during the trial.
questions.explanation: Reported commands: tell + object + to + base verb: 'told us to remain silent during the trial.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "You should hire a lawyer immediately.")
options: She suggested to hire a lawyer immediately.
She suggested hiring a lawyer immediately.
She suggested me hiring a lawyer immediately.
She suggested that I hiring a lawyer immediately.
questions.explanation: 'Suggest' is followed by a gerund or 'that + subject + base verb': 'suggested hiring a lawyer immediately.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The firm which she works for it handles criminal defense cases.
The firm for that she works handles criminal defense cases.
The firm for which she works handles criminal defense cases.
The firm she works for which handles criminal defense cases.
questions.explanation: In formal style, the preposition moves before 'which': 'the firm for which she works.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The report publishing last week revealed a rise in cybercrime.
The report published last week reveal a rise in cybercrime.
The report which published last week revealed a rise in cybercrime.
The report published last week revealed a rise in cybercrime.
questions.explanation: A passive meaning reduces 'which was published' to the past participle alone: 'The report published last week...'

questions.topic: Modal verbs of past deduction (must have)
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The thief must have entered through the back window.
The thief must entered through the back window.
The thief must have enter through the back window.
The thief must has entered through the back window.
questions.explanation: Past deduction: must have + past participle: 'must have entered through the back window.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The authorities should acted sooner to prevent the fraud.
The authorities should have acted sooner to prevent the fraud.
The authorities should have act sooner to prevent the fraud.
The authorities should has acted sooner to prevent the fraud.
questions.explanation: Past regret/criticism: should have + past participle: 'should have acted sooner.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Online fraud rose significantly over the past five years.
Online fraud has risen significantly over the past five years.
Online fraud have risen significantly over the past five years.
Online fraud have rose significantly over the past five years.
questions.explanation: 'Over the past five years' links the past to the present, so present perfect is used: 'has risen significantly.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: By the time officers arrived, the suspect fled.
By the time officers had arrived, the suspect fled.
By the time officers arrived, the suspect have already fled.
By the time officers arrived, the suspect had already fled.
questions.explanation: The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect: 'the suspect had already fled.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Lawmakers are meeting next week to discuss the new bill.
Lawmakers meet next week to discuss the new bill.
Lawmakers will meeting next week to discuss the new bill.
Lawmakers are meet next week to discuss the new bill.
questions.explanation: Present continuous expresses a fixed future arrangement: 'are meeting next week.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He said he will appeal the court's decision.
He said he would appeal the court's decision.
He said he would appealed the court's decision.
He said he would have appeal the court's decision.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, 'will' shifts back to 'would': 'he said he would appeal the decision.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I wish the justice system take fraud cases more seriously.
I wish the justice system have taken fraud cases more seriously.
I wish the justice system took fraud cases more seriously.
I wish the justice system would take fraud cases more seriously as a rule.
questions.explanation: 'Wish' + past simple expresses regret about a present situation: 'I wish the justice system took fraud cases more seriously.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I wish the bank warned us earlier about the scam.
I wish the bank have warned us earlier about the scam.
I wish the bank would have warned us earlier about the scam.
I wish the bank had warned us earlier about the scam.
questions.explanation: 'Wish' + past perfect expresses regret about the past: 'I wish the bank had warned us earlier.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We had our contract reviewed by a lawyer.
We had reviewed our contract by a lawyer.
We had our contract review by a lawyer.
We have our contract reviewed by a lawyer last year.
questions.explanation: Causative form: have + object + past participle shows someone else did the action: 'had our contract reviewed.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Never before the court had seen such a complex case.
Never before had the court seen such a complex case.
Never before did the court seen such a complex case.
Never before has the court had seen such a complex case.
questions.explanation: Negative adverbials at the start trigger inversion: 'Never before had the court seen...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The detectives are looking the case into.
The detectives are looking in to the case.
The detectives are looking into the case.
The detectives are looking into to the case.
questions.explanation: 'Look into' means 'investigate' and is inseparable: 'looking into the case.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: What the department urgently need are more trained detectives.
That the department urgently needs is more trained detectives.
What the department urgently needs is more trained detectives it.
What the department urgently needs is more trained detectives.
questions.explanation: 'What' clefts take a singular verb when the complement is singular: 'What the department needs is more trained detectives.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Some countries impose harsh penalties, whereas others favor rehabilitation.
Some countries impose harsh penalties, whereas others favors rehabilitation.
Some countries impose harsh penalties whereas, others favor rehabilitation.
Some countries impose harsh penalties despite others favor rehabilitation.
questions.explanation: 'Whereas' contrasts two clauses and is followed directly by the subject: 'whereas others favor rehabilitation.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: In spite the new evidence, the verdict remained unchanged.
In spite of the new evidence, the verdict remained unchanged.
Despite of the new evidence, the verdict remained unchanged.
In spite of the new evidence, the verdict remained unchanged though.
questions.explanation: 'In spite of' is followed by a noun phrase: 'In spite of the new evidence, the verdict remained unchanged.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: A number of reports has linked poverty to higher crime rates.
The number of reports have linked poverty to higher crime rates.
A number of reports have linked poverty to higher crime rates.
A great number of reports has linked poverty to higher crime rates.
questions.explanation: 'A number of' + plural noun takes a plural verb: 'a number of reports have linked...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She spoke in behalf of the entire legal team.
She spoke on behalf for the entire legal team.
She spoke behalf of the entire legal team.
She spoke on behalf of the entire legal team.
questions.explanation: 'On behalf of' means 'representing someone': 'she spoke on behalf of the legal team.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The enforcement of stricter penalties reduced repeat offenses significantly.
The enforce of stricter penalties reduced repeat offenses significantly.
The enforcing of stricter penalties reduced repeat offenses significantly.
The enforcement of stricter penalties reduce repeat offenses significantly.
questions.explanation: Formal writing often nominalizes verbs into nouns: 'enforce' becomes 'the enforcement of...'

questions.question: Which is the most appropriate formal opening line for an email requesting information about a legal case?
options: I'm writing to ask you about my case, ok?
I am writing to enquire about the status of my case.
Just wanted to know about my case.
Hey, tell me about my case.
questions.explanation: 'I am writing to enquire about...' is a standard formal opening for information requests.

questions.question: Which is the most appropriate opening line for a formal complaint about police misconduct?
options: I'm writing because I'm really mad about the officer's behavior.
I want to complain about the officer's behavior, it's bad.
I am writing to express my concern about an officer's conduct.
I am writing to express my concern about an officer's conduct, ok.
questions.explanation: Formal complaints use measured language such as 'I am writing to express my concern about...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The details of the fraud case were extreme alarming.
The details of the fraud case were extremely alarm.
The details of the fraud case were very much alarming.
The details of the fraud case were extremely alarming.
questions.explanation: 'Extremely' (adverb) modifies the adjective 'alarming': 'were extremely alarming.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The new law reduces sentencing disparities. Moreover, it saves taxpayer money.
The new law reduces sentencing disparities, moreover it saves taxpayer money.
The new law reduces sentencing disparities. Moreover it saves taxpayer money.
The new law reduces sentencing disparities moreover, it saves taxpayer money.
questions.explanation: 'Moreover' begins a new sentence and is followed by a comma: 'The new law reduces disparities. Moreover, it saves taxpayer money.'

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: You'd support harsher penalties for fraud, didn't you?
You'd support harsher penalties for fraud, wouldn't you?
You'd support harsher penalties for fraud, would you?
You'd support harsher penalties for fraud, wouldn't it?
questions.explanation: A positive statement with 'would' takes a negative tag: 'You'd support..., wouldn't you?'
